dervis-irab:1-8.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وِزْرَكَ): al-wizr is sin, or a heavy load. The explanation of this root has already been given.
(أَنْقَضَ): it weighed heavily. In al-Mukhtār: "The original of inqāḍ is a sound like pecking." Abū Ḥayyān said: "The lexicographers said: the load anqaḍa the back of the she-camel when you hear a creaking from it because of the heaviness of the load; and you hear the naqīḍ of the cauldron, i.e. its creaking. ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās said:
وانقض ظهري ما تطويت منهم ... وكنت عليهم مشفقا متحننا
(What I endured from them made my back creak, though I was compassionate and tender toward them.)
And Jamīl said: 'until its ropes creaked with the naqīḍ, and she was about to break with a monstrous load.'"
Al-naqīḍ is the sound of breaking apart and loosening.
The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "The verbal noun is anqaḍa yunqiḍu inqāḍan, so he is munqiḍ, and its meaning is: it weighed down your back. The Arabs say anqaḍat al-farārīj when the chicks chirp. Dhū al-Rumma said:
كأن أصوات من إيغالهنّ بنا ... أواخر الميس إنقاض الفراريج
(As if the sounds, from their pressing on with us, of the rear parts of the saddle-wood were the chirping of chicks.)
Al-naqḍ is the emaciated camel, and its plural is anqāḍ."
Al-mays is a tree from which saddles are made, and what is meant here is saddles; Dhū al-Rumma separated the muḍāf from the muḍāf ilayhi by a preposition and its genitive noun.
(فَانْصَبْ): so toil in supplication. In al-Mukhtār: "naṣiba means he toiled, and its pattern is ṭariba." In it also: "faragha min al-shughl (pattern dakhala), and also farāgh." And in it also: "raghiba fīhi: he desired it; its pattern is ṭariba, and also raghba; irtaghaba fīhi is the same; and raghiba ʿanhu: he did not desire it. One says raghghabahu fīhi targhīban and arghabahu fīhi too."

* I'rab:
(أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ وَوَضَعْنا عَنْكَ وِزْرَكَ الَّذِي أَنْقَضَ ظَهْرَكَ): The hamza is for confirmatory interrogation, that is, "We opened (it)", and for that reason a past verb is conjoined to it. Al-Rāghib said: "The original of sharḥ is the spreading out of meat and the like; one says sharaḥtu al-laḥm and sharraḥtuhu. From it comes sharḥ al-ṣadr, which is its expanding by divine light, tranquillity from Allah and a spirit from Him." (نَشْرَحْ) is an imperfect verb jussive by (لَمْ), its agent a latent pronoun, its implied form being "We" (naḥnu). (لَكَ) is attached to (نَشْرَحْ), and (صَدْرَكَ) is the direct object. Ibn Khālawayh said: "This sūra too is one of those in which Allah the Exalted enumerates His blessings upon His Prophet ﷺ and reminds him of them. When Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed: ﴿فَمَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ أَنْ يَهْدِيَهُ يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلامِ﴾, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is the chest opened?' He said: 'Yes, by a light that Allah causes to enter it.' He said: 'And what is the sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Distancing oneself from the abode of delusion, turning to the abode of permanence, and preparing for death before it passes.'" And in the hadith: "Remember death, for you are not in much without it becoming little, nor in little without it becoming much." The verbal noun is sharaḥa yashraḥu sharḥan, so he is shāriḥ and the direct object is mashrūḥ. It is said: "sharaḥa al-rajul al-jāriya" when he deflowered her. (لَكَ) is attached to (نَشْرَحْ) and (صَدْرَكَ) is the direct object. (وَوَضَعْنا) is conjoined to (أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ), (عَنْكَ) is attached to (وَضَعْنا), (وِزْرَكَ) is the direct object, and (الَّذِي) is an adjective of (الْوِزْرَ); the clause (أَنْقَضَ) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila of (الَّذِي), and (ظَهْرَكَ) is the direct object. Ibn Khālawayh said: "One says al-ẓahr, al-maṭā, al-jawz, al-matn, al-matna and al-qarā, all meaning the back. ʿUqba ibn Sābiq said:
ومتنتان خظاتان ... كزحلوق من الهضب
(and two fleshy back-muscles like a slide on a hillside.)
The flesh of the back is called al-dhanūb; the lower back is called al-qaṭāt. It is said: 'So-and-so, from his stupidity and clumsiness, does not know his laṭāt from his qaṭāt': al-laṭāt is the forehead and al-qaṭāt the lower back."
(وَرَفَعْنا لَكَ ذِكْرَكَ): Conjoined to what precedes; (لَكَ) is attached to (رَفَعْنا) and (ذِكْرَكَ) is the direct object. The preposition and its genitive noun are put before the explicit direct object here and in what preceded, though its right is to follow it, in order to hasten the delight and heighten the anticipation. The wording of Ibn Khālawayh is beautiful where he says: "The polytheists of the Arabs used to say: Muhammad is a ṣunbūr, that is, a lone man without offspring; when he dies, his remembrance is cut off. So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّ شانِئَكَ هُوَ الْأَبْتَرُ﴾, that is, the one who hates you is the abtar who has neither child nor remembrance. As for you, O Muhammad, your mention is joined to My mention until the Day of Resurrection: when the muezzin says 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah', he says 'I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'"
(فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً): The fāʾ is a conjunction upon an omitted statement that must be implied, the implied form being: "We have granted you what We granted you, so let despair not touch you, for with hardship there is ease." (إِنَّ) is a particle resembling the verb; (مَعَ الْعُسْرِ) is an adverb attached to an omitted fronted khabar; (يُسْراً) is its postponed noun. The pairing of ease with hardship is an addition to the consolation and a strengthening of the heart. (إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً) is a resumptive clause, to affirm that hardship is followed by ease. The alif-lām in (الْعُسْرِ) is for defining the genus, and in the second it is for previous mention; for that reason it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them: "One hardship will never overcome two eases." The reason is that when the Arabs bring a noun and then repeat it with the alif-lām, it is the first, as in "A man came, and I honoured the man", and as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿كَما أَرْسَلْنا إِلى فِرْعَوْنَ رَسُولًا فَعَصى فِرْعَوْنُ الرَّسُولَ﴾; and if you repeat it without alif-lām, it is other than the first. So in His saying ﴿إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً﴾, when He repeated the second hardship He repeated it with the alif-lām, and since the second ease was other than the first, He did not repeat it with the alif-lām. The wording of al-Zamakhsharī: "If you say: what is the meaning of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them, 'One hardship will never overcome two eases', when it has been reported as a raised report (marfūʿ) that he ﷺ went out one day laughing and saying 'One hardship will never overcome two eases'? I say: this is taken at face value and built upon strength of hope, and the promise of Allah is to be carried only on the fullest and most complete that the wording can bear. The statement about it is that it is possible that the second sentence is a repetition of the first, as He repeated ﴿وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِينَ﴾, to establish its meaning in souls and fix it in hearts, as a single word is repeated in your saying 'Zayd came to me, Zayd'; and possible that the first is a promise that hardship is certainly followed by ease, and the second a new promise that hardship is followed by ease, so they are two eases on the assumption of resumption. Hardship is one because it cannot be otherwise: either its definiteness is for previous mention, and it is the hardship they were in, so it is the same, since its ruling is the ruling of Zayd in your saying 'With Zayd is money, with Zayd is money'; or it is for the genus which everyone knows, so it is the same too. As for ease, it is indefinite, covering part of the genus; and if the second speech is resumptive, not a repetition, it covers a part other than the first part, without difficulty. If you say: what is meant by the two eases? I say: it may be that what is meant is what was made easy for them of conquests in the days of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and what was made easy for them in the days of the caliphs; or the ease of this world and the ease of the next, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿قُلْ هَلْ تَرَبَّصُونَ بِنا إِلَّا إِحْدَى الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ﴾, which are the good of victory and the good of reward. If you say: what is the meaning of this indefiniteness? I say: magnification, as if it were said: with hardship there is a great ease."
Abū al-Baqāʾ said: "Hardship in both places is one, because the alif-lām requires repetition of the first. As for ease in both places, they are two, because when an indefinite is meant to be repeated, its pronoun or the alif-lām is brought. From this was said: 'One hardship will never overcome two eases.'"
The wording of Ibn Khālawayh: "Ibn ʿAbbās said: one hardship does not overcome two eases. The explanation of this is that in ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ﴾ there is one hardship and two eases, although it is repeated in wording, because the second hardship is the first hardship, while the second ease is other than the first because it is indefinite; and an indefinite, when repeated, is repeated with alif-lām, as in your saying 'A man came to me and I honoured the man'. So when He mentioned ease twice and did not put alif-lām into the second, it was known that the second is other than the first." Ibn Hishām said in his delightful book Mughnī al-Labīb, in Chapter Six of the book, on warning against matters that have become widespread among the parsers while the correct view is the opposite: "The fourteenth is their saying that when an indefinite is repeated as indefinite it is other than the first, and when it is repeated as definite, or a definite is repeated as definite or as indefinite, the second is identical with the first. They took on this basis what was reported: 'One hardship will never overcome two eases.' Al-Zajjāj said: He mentioned hardship with the alif-lām and then repeated its mention, so the meaning became: with hardship there are two eases. Witness for the first two forms is that you say 'I bought a horse and then I sold a horse', so the second is other than the first, whereas if you said 'then I sold the horse', the second would be the first itself; and for the fourth form is the saying of the Ḥamāsa poet:
صفحنا عن بني ذهل ... وقلنا القوم إخوان
عسى الأيام أن يرجعن ... قوما كالذي كانوا
(We pardoned the Banū Dhuhl, and we said: the folk are brothers; perhaps the days will return a people as they once were.)
Three matters make this problematic. One: the apparent sense in the verse ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ﴾ is that the second sentence is a repetition of the first, as you say 'Zayd has a house, Zayd has a house'; accordingly, the second is identical with the first. Two: Ibn Masʿūd said, 'If hardship were in a hole, ease would seek it until it entered upon it; one hardship will never overcome two eases', although the verse in his reading and in his codex occurs once only; this shows what we claimed concerning emphasis, and that he did not derive the repetition of ease from its being repeated, but from something else, perhaps having understood it from the magnification in the indefiniteness, and so interpreted it as the ease of the two abodes. Three: in the Revelation there are verses that refute these four rulings. The first is problematic in light of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ مِنْ ضَعْفٍ﴾ (the verse), and ﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي فِي السَّماءِ إِلهٌ وَفِي الْأَرْضِ إِلهٌ﴾, and ﴿وَاللَّهُ إِلهٌ واحِدٌ سُبْحانَهُ﴾. The second, in light of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما أَنْ يُصْلِحا بَيْنَهُما صُلْحاً وَالصُّلْحُ خَيْرٌ﴾, for the first ṣulḥ is specific, being the reconciliation between spouses, while the second is general; for this reason this verse is cited as evidence for the recommendation of every permissible reconciliation; and similarly ﴿زِدْناهُمْ عَذاباً فَوْقَ الْعَذابِ﴾, for a thing cannot be above itself... And the fourth: ﴿يَسْأَلُكَ أَهْلُ الْكِتابِ أَنْ تُنَزِّلَ عَلَيْهِمْ كِتاباً مِنَ السَّماءِ﴾ and the saying: 'When people are people and time is time', for if the second were equal to the first in its sense, there would be no benefit in the predication about it; this is from the category of his saying 'I am Abū al-Najm and my poetry is my poetry', i.e. my poetry has not changed from its state. If it is claimed that the rule concerning them holds only in the absence of an indication, whereas if an indication exists then relying on it is easy..." Then Ibn Hishām cited the words of al-Zamakhsharī mentioned above. And al-Taftāzānī said in al-Talwīḥ: "Know that what is meant is that this is the default when unrestricted and when the context lacks an indication; otherwise an indefinite is sometimes repeated as indefinite without any difference, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي فِي السَّماءِ إِلهٌ وَفِي الْأَرْضِ إِلهٌ﴾, and ﴿وَقالُوا لَوْلا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ آيَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ قُلْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ قادِرٌ عَلى أَنْ يُنَزِّلَ آيَةً﴾, and ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ مِنْ ضَعْفٍ ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنْ بَعْدِ ضَعْفٍ قُوَّةً ثُمَّ جَعَلَ مِنْ بَعْدِ قُوَّةٍ ضَعْفاً وَشَيْبَةً﴾, meaning the strength of youth; and from this is the category of verbal emphasis. An indefinite is sometimes repeated as definite with a difference, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَهذا كِتابٌ أَنْزَلْناهُ مُبارَكٌ﴾, then He said ﴿أَنْ تَقُولُوا إِنَّما أُنْزِلَ الْكِتابُ عَلى طائِفَتَيْنِ مِنْ قَبْلِنا﴾. A definite is sometimes repeated as indefinite without difference, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إِنَّما إِلهُكُمْ إِلهٌ واحِدٌ﴾, and the like in speech is plentiful, such as their saying 'knowledge is such-and-such knowledge', and 'I entered the house and saw the house of so-and-so', and among it is the verse of the Ḥamāsa poet."
After having cited the sayings of the imams on this question, we summarise it for you in a useful summary, and say: 1- If a noun is repeated twice and both are indefinite, the second is other than the first. 2- If both are definite, or only the second, it is identical with it. 3- If the first is definite and the second indefinite, there are two views. The first and the second are like hardship and ease in His saying ﴿فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْراً﴾; the third is like ﴿فِيها مِصْباحٌ الْمِصْباحُ﴾; and the fourth as in his saying "We pardoned the Banū Dhuhl" (the two verses). This rule is a majority rule, as the words of the imams cited above indicate. Ibn al-Subkī clarified this difficulty in a statement that fell upon us as rain upon the thirsty, and this is its text: "It appears that this rule is not firmly established, because it is broken by many examples, among them with two definites: ﴿هَلْ جَزاءُ الْإِحْسانِ إِلَّا الْإِحْسانُ﴾, for the first is the deed and the second is the reward; and in the definiteness of the second also ﴿وَما يَتَّبِعُ أَكْثَرُهُمْ إِلَّا ظَنًّا إِنَّ الظَّنَّ لا يُغْنِي﴾, for what is meant by the second is the generality of conjecture, not the first; and with two indefinites: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرامِ قِتالٍ فِيهِ قُلْ قِتالٌ فِيهِ كَبِيرٌ﴾, for the second is the first." After writing the above, and having nearly been satisfied with the solution of Ibn al-Subkī, a comment on these objections occurred to us: it appears that these verses do not depart from the rule upon reflection. The lām in al-iḥsān, as appears, is for the genus, not for previous mention, as Ibn al-Subkī said, and then in meaning it is like an indefinite; unlike the verse of hardship, where the al is either for a mental precedent, namely the severity from the unbelievers that came upon him ﷺ and upon the Muslims, or for totality, as the hadith indicates, which has been mentioned before. Likewise the verse on conjecture: we do not concede that the second is other than the first; rather it is certainly the first itself, since not every conjecture is blameworthy, how could it be, when the rulings of the law are conjectural. Likewise the verse on reconciliation: nothing prevents what is meant by it from being the mentioned reconciliation, which is between spouses; and the approval of reconciliation in all matters is not taken from the sunna or from the verse by way of analogy; indeed it is not permissible to say the verse is general and that every reconciliation is good, because a reconciliation that makes the forbidden permitted or the permitted forbidden is prohibited. Likewise the verse on fighting: the second in it is without doubt not identical with the first, because the fighting asked about is the fighting that occurred in the expedition of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī in the year 2 of the Hijra, since it was the occasion of the revelation of the verse, and what is meant by the second is the genus of fighting, not that particular fighting; so consider this and resolve what has troubled you. If you say: what will you do with the verse ﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي فِي السَّماءِ إِلهٌ وَفِي الْأَرْضِ إِلهٌ﴾? Do you not see that you have neglected to discuss it? I say: Ibn al-Subkī himself said: His saying "ilāh" in the verse means "worshipped", and a derived noun is intended only for the attribute it contains; so when you say "Zayd is striking ʿAmr and striking Bakr", it is not imagined that the second is the first, although both are predicated of one person, for what is truly mentioned is the two strikings, not the two strikers, and there is no doubt that the two strikings differ. From here we conclude that the two indefinites in the verse intend nothing but the attribute, which is worship, and there is no doubt that the two acts of worship differ; so the second indefinite is other than the first in terms of what is intended, even though they apply to one entity. So the verse too does not depart from the rule.
(فَإِذا فَرَغْتَ فَانْصَبْ وَإِلى رَبِّكَ فَارْغَبْ): The fāʾ is a conjunction upon an implied statement that the context deserves; you may also make it resumptive, as if it were an answer to a question that arose, namely: what comes after thanks, worship and striving in them? So He said: "when you have finished", that is, from the prayer and other kinds of worship. From al-Ḥasan: "when you have finished from the expedition, strive in worship." But this conflicts with the sūra's being Meccan, for the command to fight came only after the Hijra; so perhaps it is the interpretation of Ibn ʿAbbās, who held that the sūra is Medinan. (إِذا) is an adverb of future time containing the meaning of condition, attached to the apodosis. The clause (فَرَغْتَ) is in the position of a genitive, through the annexation of the adverb to it. The fāʾ links the apodosis. (انْصَبْ) is an imperative verb and a latent agent, and the clause has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of a non-jussive conditional. (إِلى رَبِّكَ) is attached to (ارْغَبْ), and the fāʾ does not prevent that. (ارْغَبْ) is an imperative verb, and the clause is conjoined to the one before it.

* Rhetoric:
In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَوَضَعْنا عَنْكَ وِزْرَكَ الَّذِي أَنْقَضَ ظَهْرَكَ﴾ there is an illustrative metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya), by which is meant his ﷺ protection from sin, where there is no sin. His state, as he labours under what he imagines to be a burden of sin though it is not, is likened to the state of one whom a heavy load has bowed and whom effort and scorching heat have worn out, so that he walks exhausted and distressed, almost falling from the weight of what he strains to carry. The removal of the burden is a kināya for his protection and purification ﷺ from the stain of sins. In carrying out this metaphor we say: his state is likened to the state of one whom the load has bent, sweat has covered, and effort has worn out, until, when the load is put down from him, he breathes a sigh of relief and the griefs and terrors are removed from him, the common ground being that each of them is exhausted and distressed by what he carries, finds it burdensome and complains of it, and longs for it to be lifted from his shoulder. Then the structure indicating the state of the thing likened to was borrowed for the thing likened, by way of illustrative metaphor, and the indication is circumstantial.
